text: The Terraform & Bicep course taught provider blocks, resource blocks, state, and the plan-apply workflow against Azure resources. This lesson applies those exact same mechanics to a provider you haven't used yet: Snowflake itself. The concepts don't change -- only the provider and its resource types do.

The Snowflake-Labs provider block looks just like any other Terraform provider -- authentication comes from environment variables in CI, never hardcoded in the dot-tf files themselves, the same secrets discipline from the CI/CD lesson.

Everything you ran as a one-off SQL statement in earlier lessons has a direct resource equivalent. The database resource sets its Time Travel retention right here, provisioned from day one -- tying directly into the disaster-recovery lesson ahead. Both warehouses get their size and auto-suspend defined in code too.

DRIFTWOOD_ETL_WH and DRIFTWOOD_BI_WH get different auto_suspend values deliberately -- they're genuinely different workloads. The ETL warehouse runs in a tight daily burst and should suspend fast, at sixty seconds. The BI warehouse serves sporadic analyst queries throughout the day and benefits from staying warm longer, at three hundred.

Roles and grants are resources too. The analyst role gets SELECT on every table in the marts schema specifically -- the same marts-only, least-privilege boundary the RBAC lesson defined, now enforced in version-controlled code instead of a one-off GRANT statement someone might forget to repeat.

Terraform provisions the infrastructure -- databases, warehouses, roles, grants. It never provisions the data itself, and it never runs dbt models. And it ties directly into the CI/CD pipeline: a pull request changing any dot-tf file runs terraform plan for review; only a merge to main runs terraform apply.
Next lesson: monitoring pipeline health and warehouse cost -- catching a problem before it becomes a surprise bill.
